# Court archive preservation

This field note explains paper court record preservation. Its central process is acidic paper embrittlement and damage from moisture. Practitioners pay attention to the surrounding conditions before interpreting a single observation. A useful working method involves acid-free folders in a cool stable storage room. This is not simply a matter of collecting a number: observations need enough context to distinguish a persistent pattern from a temporary change.

An important interpretation is that remove metal fasteners when it can be done without tearing pages. For a practical assessment, document when and where the observation was made, the equipment or materials involved, and any unusual conditions. Compare measurements taken using the same method rather than assuming that unrelated measurements are directly comparable. Recording changes over time also helps explain whether an intervention is having its intended effect.

There is an important limitation: digitization improves access but does not replace physical preservation. When conditions change, revisit the original assumptions instead of applying the same response automatically. A careful operator checks equipment, records the relevant circumstances, and looks for independent evidence before drawing conclusions. Reports should distinguish what was observed from what is inferred and describe any uncertainty that could affect the decision.

The best procedure depends on the actual situation and the people responsible for it. Where a result has consequences for safety, conservation, or expensive equipment, use the appropriate local guidance and consult a qualified specialist. The examples in this note illustrate the principles rather than providing an exhaustive operating manual.
